text: What if Russia never sold Alaska?
Russian troops would be guarding the Canadian border. And Soviet missiles would sit on North American soil.
But in the real world, in eighteen-sixty-seven, Russia sold it to the United States for just seven-point-two million-dollars.
That's more land than Texas, California and Montana combined.
So why did Russia sell? And if it hadn't, what would the world look like today? Let's find out.
First, a geography lesson. Russia and America are neighbors. At its narrowest, the Bering Strait is only about fifty miles wide.
In the middle sit two islands. One is Russian, one is American. They're less than three miles apart.
In seventeen-forty-one, a Danish captain working for the Tsar, Vitus Bering, sailed across and reached the coast of Alaska.
His crew brought back sea otter pelts. The softest fur in the world, and China paid a fortune for it.
Word spread fast. Russian fur traders poured across the sea and hunted their way along the Aleutian Islands.
The people who had lived there for thousands of years, like the Aleut and the Tlingit, were forced to hunt for them, and many times they fought back.
In seventeen-ninety-nine, the Tsar created the Russian-American Company, a private monopoly that ran the colony for the state.
Its capital was Sitka. Churches, a fort, a shipyard. By the eighteen-thirties, more than one-thousand people lived there.
Russia even reached California. Fort Ross stood about ninety miles north of San Francisco.
But for all that land, there were never more than about eight-hundred Russians living there.
So why sell? Three reasons.
One. The sea otters were almost gone. The money machine was running dry.
Two. It was too far away. From Saint Petersburg, across Siberia, to Alaska could take months.
And three, the big one. Britain.
In eighteen-fifty-three, Russia went to war against Britain and France in Crimea. And lost.
During that war, an Anglo-French fleet sailed all the way to Russia's Pacific port on Kamchatka and attacked it.
The lesson was clear. In the next war, Britain could march in from Canada and take Alaska, and Russia couldn't stop it.
And Russia was broke after the war. If you're going to lose it anyway, you might as well get paid.
Sell it to whom? To the enemy of your enemy. The United States, which had its own grudges against Britain.
But the deal had to wait. America was busy fighting its own Civil War.
When the war ended, one American wanted Alaska badly. Secretary of State William Seward.
The Russian minister came to his house one evening. Seward didn't wait for morning. He opened up the State Department that night.
Before dawn on March thirtieth, eighteen-sixty-seven, the treaty was signed.
The price: seven-point-two million-dollars. About two cents an acre.
Critics called it Seward's Icebox. But here's the thing: most newspapers at the time actually supported the deal.
Quick quiz. When the Senate voted on the treaty, how many senators voted no? Two, twelve, or twenty?
Just two. It passed thirty-seven to two.
On October eighteenth, eighteen-sixty-seven, in Sitka, the Russian flag came down and the American flag went up.
Thirty years later, gold was found in the Klondike, and tens of thousands of Americans rushed north through Alaska.
And in nineteen-sixty-eight, oil at Prudhoe Bay. The biggest oil field in North America. Not a bad return on seven-point-two million-dollars.
But this deal almost didn't happen. If Seward hadn't been in office, if the Civil War had dragged on, or if the Tsar had changed his mind.
So let's go back to eighteen-sixty-seven, and tear up that treaty.
From here, there are two paths. The most likely one. And the scariest one.
Path A. Russia's worst fear comes true.
In that very same year, eighteen-sixty-seven, Canada was born as a country under the British Crown.
Many historians think that in the next war between Russia and Britain, Alaska would have fallen to the British within a few decades.
And in the end, Alaska would simply become part of Canada.
Canada would grow by about a sixth, and it would own both the Klondike gold road and Prudhoe Bay oil.
America would have no Arctic coast at all. And in World War Two, there would be no northern route to fly nearly eight-thousand warplanes to the Soviets.
In the real world, Japan seized the Alaskan islands of Attu and Kiska in nineteen-forty-two. In Path A, that's Canada's fight.
Path A sounds quiet. But it changes one thing forever. America would no longer be Russia's neighbor.
Path B. Britain never comes, and Russia hangs on to Alaska, all the way to nineteen-seventeen.
That year, revolution. The Tsar is overthrown, and a civil war follows.
In the real world, America actually sent about eight-thousand troops into Siberia, landing at Vladivostok.
In Path B, America might grab Alaska in the chaos. But let's say it fails, and the Reds win.
Now the Soviet Union owns a piece of North America, with a land border to Canada over one-thousand-five-hundred miles long.
In nineteen-sixty-two, the Soviets put missiles in Cuba, ninety miles from Florida, and the world came close to nuclear war.
In Path B, there's nothing to smuggle. The missiles are already on Soviet soil, less than one-thousand miles from Seattle.
Prudhoe Bay oil would pay for the Red Army, not for America.
And Canada becomes the front line of the Cold War, like West Germany in our world.
America would have to pour its troops and money into defending its own continent.
So what would that mean for you?
At its peak in nineteen-eighty-eight, Alaska's North Slope pumped about a quarter of all the oil produced in the United States.
Since nineteen-eighty-two, every Alaskan has received a yearly check from that oil money. The Permanent Fund Dividend.
About six out of every ten pounds of wild seafood caught in the US comes from Alaskan waters.
And today, most of America's long-range missile interceptors are based in Alaska, at Fort Greely, guarding the whole country.
In Path B, every one of those flips. The oil, the fish, the shield. Instead of protecting you, that land would be aimed at you.
Back to the real world.
Russia sold because it knew it couldn't keep Alaska. Better to get paid than lose it to Britain for nothing. At the time, it made sense.
America got more than gold and oil. It got a front door to the Pacific and the Arctic.
And without the deal, the likely ending is a Canadian Alaska. The scary one is the Soviets in North America.
So, if you were the Tsar in eighteen-sixty-seven, would you have sold? Tell me in the comments.
Next time: what if Napoleon never sold Louisiana, and half of America stayed French?
